criterion_notes.c1: Fails C1 (and triggers Exclusion Criteria 7 and 8): the paper examines agro-industrial land and bulk irrigation water resource 'grabs' by the sugarcane and ethanol sector in Valle del Cauca rather than household or community water or sanitation service access. Dry-season municipal water shortages and displaced rural farmers having to buy household water are mentioned only anecdotally in two brief passages on page 11 as externalities of agricultural irrigation extraction.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2 in isolation, the paper examines governance and regulatory factors—specifically the Bonsucro private multi-stakeholder biofuel certification standard, national biofuel blending mandates, and bulk water-resource extraction concessions and pollution rules administered by the Cauca Valley Corporation (CVC)—though overall full-text eligibility under the plain reading still fails (plain_criterion2_decision = exclude) because these mechanisms govern agro-industrial biofuel production and agricultural water-resource capture rather than household/community WASH services (Exclusion Criteria 7 and 8). Under the active narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, the paper clearly fails C2 (c2 = no): Bonsucro certification metrics for sugar mills/cane growers and bulk agricultural irrigation concessions are not rule-type legal or administrative mechanisms directly governing household or community water or sanitation service access (such as household eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation rules for utility connection, household tariffs, utility enforcement/discretion, or water utility regulatory structure).
criterion_notes.c3: Satisfies C3: empirical qualitative case study drawing on in-depth exploratory interviews conducted between June and August 2012 with 14 sugarcane and ethanol sector stakeholders in Valle del Cauca (plus interviews with rural community residents noted on page 11), paired with document analysis of Bonsucro standards and secondary regional water data.
criterion_notes.c4: Unclear for C4: the primary outcomes examined are how the Colombian sugar industry frames and operationalizes Bonsucro certification and consolidates control over agricultural land and irrigation water concessions. Page 11 includes brief, unquantified interviewee statements about dry-season municipal water shortages and rural residents forced to buy household water, without systematic assessment of a household service-access outcome.
criterion_notes.c5: Unclear for C5 with respect to household water access: while the qualitative case study design, industry stakeholder sample (n = 14), and biofuel-certification exposure are identifiable for the agro-industrial governance study, the sample size, selection, and service-level exposure/outcome definitions for the 'other residents in rural communities' mentioned on page 11 are not reported.
criterion_notes.c6: Satisfies C6: full text is written in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: Bonsucro (2013) is the principal MSI that focuses on sustainability standards for sugar and sugarcane ethanol production.
The paper draws on in-depth exploratory interviews with 14 stakeholders in the sugarcane and ethanol industry in the Valle del Cauca region in southwest Colombia between June and August 2012.

Other interviews highlighted how the industry is attempting to change the status of ground water in the Valle del Cauca to be non-potable so that it is not available for household uses anymore and can instead become available for the sugar industry.
The municipalities that depend on underground water suffer in the dry seasons from shortages in the water supply because the water is being robbed by the sugar industry, and with license of CVC.
they now face in accessing water for household use, and how they are forced to buy water for household use.

Consequently, Bonsucro reinforces existing land ownership patterns and privileged access to cheap water concessions, and is helping to facilitate the expansion of the agro-industrial model of sugarcane production into new agricultural frontiers.

raw_response.exposure: Bonsucro multi-stakeholder biofuel sustainability certification standards, Colombian national biofuel policy mandates, and regional agricultural water-resource concessions and environmental regulation (Cauca Valley Corporation)
raw_response.outcome: Framing and implementation of Bonsucro certification by the Colombian sugarcane/ethanol industry, concentration of agricultural land and irrigation water concessions by large-scale producers, and anecdotal reports of dry-season municipal water shortages and displaced rural residents buying water for household use
raw_response.population_and_sample: 14 stakeholders in the sugarcane and ethanol industry in the Valle del Cauca region of southwest Colombia (farmers, union activists, local government officials, officials from sugar industry associations Asocana and Procana, sugar refineries, and research agronomists) interviewed June-August 2012, plus an unspecified number of rural community residents
raw_response.rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic; see also Exclusion Criteria 7 and 8 on water-resource and industrial water-access studies). This qualitative political-ecology study examines how Colombia's sugarcane and ethanol industry frames and uses Bonsucro private biofuel sustainability certification alongside state biofuel mandates and regional irrigation water concessions to consolidate control over agricultural land and bulk water resources ('land and water grabs'). Although interviewees on page 11 briefly note that agro-industrial water extraction contributes to dry-season municipal water shortages and forces displaced smallholders to buy household water, the paper does not study household or community water or sanitation service delivery or a rule-type legal/administrative mechanism directly governing household/community service access (failing C1 and C2 under the 2026-10-13 rule-type scope, and remaining excluded even under the plain C2 reading due to its agro-industrial biofuel/water-resource focus).
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative exploratory case study (semi-structured stakeholder interviews and document/policy analysis)
